American Epilepsy Society/Congress of Neurological Surgeons Epilepsy Surgery Clinical Practice Guideline

Gonzalez-Martinez J, Bergey G, Roldán-Benítez YM et al. · 2026 Oct 26
Study Type: Clinical practice guideline (AES/CNS) using GRADE methodology; multidisciplinary panel with systematic literature review. Update of the 2003 AAN practice parameters.
Key Question: What are the evidence-based recommendations for surgical treatment of epilepsy in adults and children, covering resective surgery, hypothalamic hamartoma surgery, and callosotomy?
Key Findings:
  • Scope: resective surgery for mesial temporal and neocortical epilepsy; resection/disconnection for hypothalamic hamartoma; callosotomy in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies. Neurostimulation was intentionally excluded.
  • Critical outcomes were seizure control, quality of life, mortality, adverse events, and verbal memory loss. Other neuropsychological (naming, fluency), neuropsychiatric, and social outcomes were rated important.
  • The abstract does not report the specific recommendations, strength of recommendation, or certainty of evidence.
Clinical Relevance: As the first major update in over two decades, it is likely to inform UK surgical selection and counselling, including the weighting of cognitive and quality-of-life outcomes alongside seizure freedom, though NHS pathways and commissioning criteria may differ from US practice.
Limitations: The abstract gives no recommendations or evidence grades, so the full text must be reviewed to assess applicability; the exclusion of neurostimulation also leaves a gap for patients not suited to resection.

Neurosurgery

Association Between Craniotomy and Outcomes in Patients With Acute Subdural Hematoma: Analysis of a Nationwide Trauma Registry in Japan

Shibahashi K, Inoue K, Kato T et al. · 2026 Oct 30
Study Type: Retrospective multicentre cohort study (national trauma registry, Japan Trauma Data Bank, 2019–2023) with 1:1 propensity score matching.
Key Question: Is craniotomy associated with improved survival and neurological outcome in adults with large acute subdural haematoma (>50 cm³, >1 cm thick) across the GCS 6–15 range?
Key Findings:
  • Among 610 matched pairs (from 1808 patients, median age 79), craniotomy was associated with higher survival to discharge (77.2% vs 62.6%; difference 14.7%, 95% CI 9.6–19.8%).
  • No difference in favourable neurological outcome at discharge (16.1% vs 17.9%; difference −1.9%, 95% CI −7.5 to 3.7%).
  • Survival benefit was greater in those ≥65 years (17.1% vs 3.9% if <65) and GCS 6–12 (27.8%); GCS 13–15 showed a non-beneficial point estimate (−6.1%).
Clinical Relevance: Supports individualised operative decision-making beyond haematoma thickness, relevant to UK practice with an ageing ASDH population and uncertainty about surgery in higher-GCS patients.
Limitations: Observational design with residual confounding (e.g. frailty, anticoagulation, pupil status), and only in-hospital outcomes were assessed, so long-term function and causality remain uncertain.

Journal of Neurosurgery

Stage 2 DBS without the wait: safety of same-day low-amplitude activation in a predominantly unilateral cohort

Uppalapati SC, Qushair FA, Bentley JN et al. · 2026 Oct 30
Study Type: Retrospective single-centre propensity score-adjusted cohort study (561 consecutive stage 2 DBS procedures, 2019-2024; ≥6 months' follow-up).
Key Question: Is same-day low-amplitude DBS activation at stage 2 surgery as safe as the historical delayed-programming pathway?
Key Findings:
  • Immediate activation met the noninferiority criterion in propensity-adjusted analysis (upper 95% CI for risk difference <5%). Unadjusted 6-month composite adverse events: 3.8% (11/288) immediate vs 20.5% (56/273) delayed (RD -16.7%, 95% CI -22.0 to -11.4). No device-related deaths.
  • Settings retention at 6 months after first full programming visit: 78.5% vs 54.9%; time to first change favoured immediate activation (HR 2.28, 95% CI 1.89-2.73 for delayed).
  • Exploratory: bilateral cases had more short-term speech and altered mental status events; infection, haemorrhage, erosion and lead migration did not differ.
Clinical Relevance: Offers a potential way to shorten the no-stimulation interval and reduce early programming visits, though NHS applicability depends on programming capacity and case mix (largely unilateral).
Limitations: Retrospective, non-randomised design with historical controls (temporal confounding) and no evidence on full therapeutic activation or motor efficacy.

World Neurosurgery

Calibrated Microspheres versus Liquid Embolic Agents for Chronic Subdural Hematoma: A Single-Center Clinicoradiologic Analysis

McClanahan A, Vilanilam G, Rezayev A et al. · 2026 Oct 23
Study Type: Single-centre retrospective cohort study (MMA-level analysis)
Key Question: Do outcomes after middle meningeal artery embolization (MMAe) for chronic subdural haematoma differ between 75 μm Embozene microspheres and liquid embolics (NBCA/Onyx 18)?
Key Findings:
  • Embolization failure: 5/34 (particle) vs 4/32 (liquid). Unplanned evacuation: 3/34 vs 1/32. Events were too few for meaningful comparison and no significance testing was reported for these outcomes.
  • Early SDH thickness was similar (8 vs 6 mm, P = 0.340). The particle group had more females (47% vs 19%, P = 0.020).
  • Safety cohort (n = 67): one fatal posterior-circulation infarct after Embozene (1/35 vs 0/32); no other periprocedural complications.
Clinical Relevance: Liquid embolics underpin the landmark RCTs, so this limited evidence offers no basis for preferring particles over liquids when UK units choose embolic agents or consider local protocols.
Limitations: Retrospective, non-randomised design with discretionary agent selection, baseline imbalances, and very few events leaves the study underpowered to detect real differences.

World Neurosurgery

Middle Meningeal Artery Embolization for Chronic Subdural Hematoma: A Single-Center Retrospective Direct Comparison of Squid 12 and Magic Glue

Alsabbagh M, Simkina D, Solomannikov V et al. · 2026 Oct 26
Study Type: Single-centre retrospective cohort study (194 procedures, 147 patients)
Key Question: Does the choice of liquid embolic (Squid 12 [EVOH] vs Magic Glue [cyanoacrylate]) affect unplanned repeat surgical evacuation after MMAE for chronic subdural haematoma?
Key Findings:
  • Unadjusted reoperation was higher with Squid 12 than Magic Glue: 15/118 (13%) vs 3/76 (4%); RR 0.31 for Magic Glue (95% CI 0.10–0.96; p=0.040). Sensitivity analysis was similar (RR 0.26; 95% CI 0.06–0.97).
  • Embolic agent was not independently associated with reoperation in exploratory multivariable GEE analysis.
  • Baseline hematoma thickness differed between groups (median 18 mm Squid 12 vs 12 mm Magic Glue).
Clinical Relevance: Offers no evidence to guide agent choice in UK MMAE practice, though it highlights the need for prospective comparison as MMAE use expands.
Limitations: Retrospective, non-randomised design with imbalanced baselines and only 18 reoperation events, leaving the study underpowered for adjusted analysis; authors describe findings as hypothesis-generating.

Neurosurgery

Machine Learning Prediction of Treatment Failure After Middle Meningeal Artery Embolization for Subdural Hematoma

DeMessie B, Essibayi MA, Salim HA et al. · 2026 Oct 23
Study Type: International multi-institutional retrospective cohort study with machine learning model development and internal validation.
Key Question: Can an ML model predict treatment failure (rescue surgery or retreatment for persistent/recurrent SDH) after middle meningeal artery embolization?
Key Findings:
  • Treatment failure occurred in 9.2% (64/692) of hematomas in the test cohort. The gradient boosting model achieved AUC 0.832 (95% CI 0.766–0.889) after calibration; Brier score 0.053.
  • Strongest predictors were age–platelet interaction, platelet–haemoglobin ratio, platelet count, SDH thickness and age.
  • Observed failure was 1.6% (low-risk, <5%), 6.0% (medium-risk) and 59.6% (high-risk, >15%), a 37.2-fold difference. Only 7.5% of hematomas were high-risk.
Clinical Relevance: Could inform patient selection, counselling and follow-up intensity as MMAE use grows in UK practice, though not yet ready for routine clinical use.
Limitations: Retrospective design with internal validation only; no external validation cohort and a high-risk group of only 52 hematomas, so estimates may be unstable.

Acta Neurochirurgica

Need for a definitive trial of local versus general anaesthesia in chronic subdural haematoma; survey and literature review of ongoing trials

Stubbs DJ, Gillespie CS, Watson ML et al. · 2026 Jul 28
Study Type: Mixed-methods evidence review: trial registry search, Cochrane database review, and survey of anaesthetists and neurosurgeons.
Key Question: Is there sufficient evidence to guide choice between local (± sedation) and general anaesthesia for cSDH surgery, and what would a definitive trial need to address?
Key Findings:
  • Few high-quality studies exist, particularly RCTs, comparing LAS with GA in cSDH surgery.
  • Existing literature and practitioner survey responses suggest LAS may give equivalent outcomes, but current studies are significantly confounded.
  • All registered trials are single-centre; Cochrane reviews from other surgical fields highlight equipoise, trial design, and outcome selection as key barriers. The abstract gives no quantitative data (e.g. survey response numbers or effect sizes).
Clinical Relevance: cSDH commonly affects frail, comorbid patients, so a multicentre UK trial on anaesthetic technique is clearly needed, and this paper supports its feasibility and design considerations.
Limitations: Findings rest on a narrative review and survey rather than systematic synthesis; survey size, response rate, and representativeness are not reported in the abstract.

Acta Neurochirurgica

Dual-step burr hole with periosteal anchoring technique: a robust method for ventricular catheter fixation - how I do it

Hu Y, Qin Y, Liang J et al. · 2026 Aug 03
Study Type: Technical note ("how I do it"); no patient cohort or comparative data reported.
Key Question: Can a dual-step burr hole combined with periosteal anchoring improve fixation of proximal ventricular catheters in VPS and Ommaya reservoir insertion?
Key Findings:
  • Technique: a shallow outer burr hole seats a right-angle catheter guide, and a smaller central inner burr hole exposes the dura for catheter passage.
  • The connector is sutured to preserved pericranium with nonabsorbable sutures, and the periosteal flap is then reapproximated.
  • The authors propose this creates a multiplanar mechanical barrier against migration and kinking. No outcome data (migration, revision or infection rates, follow-up) are provided in the abstract.
Clinical Relevance: Proximal catheter migration and obstruction drive shunt revision burden in NHS practice, so a simple, low-cost fixation option may interest surgeons seeking to reduce avoidable reoperations.
Limitations: No reported patient numbers, outcomes or comparison with standard fixation, so the claimed robustness is unsubstantiated by clinical evidence.
